\chapter{Afternoon}
\label{ch:ml-afternoon}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say afternoon in Malayalam as uchakaḻiññ -- literally 'noon having passed'.}

Build uchakaḻiññ from ucha plus kaḻiyuka, and contrast it with Telugu, which widened its noon-word instead.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ml{ഉച്ചകഴിഞ്ഞ്}]{\ml{ഉച്ചകഴിഞ്ഞ്} (uchakaḻiññ) — \textquotedblleft{}noon, having passed\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C28-uchakazhinju}



\begin{quote}
Telugu let its noon-word quietly widen to also mean \textquotedblleft{}afternoon.\textquotedblright{} Malayalam solves the same problem with a completely different strategy: it builds a new phrase instead.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{ഉച്ചകഴിഞ്ഞ്}} (\textbf{uchakaḻiññ}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{afternoon}\textquotedblright{} — is a transparent \textbf{two-word phrase}, not a single dictionary headword (no Wiktionary entry exists for the compound as a whole). It's built from \textbf{\ml{ഉച്ച}} (already met, Chapter 17, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{noon}\textquotedblright{}) plus \textbf{\ml{കഴിഞ്ഞ്}}, the \textbf{past converb form} of \textbf{\ml{കഴിയുക}} (\emph{kaḻiyuka}), itself Wiktionary-confirmed \textbf{Proto-Dravidian} \emph{\textbf{*kaẓi}} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to be over, spent, finished}\textquotedblright{}). Be honest about the citation: Wiktionary's own conjugation line shows only the finite past tense, \textbf{\ml{കഴിഞ്ഞു}} (\emph{kaḻiññu}) — not this converb form directly. The converb is the grammatically correct choice for chaining into a compound like this one, but treat the exact written form as a reasonable grammatical inference, not a directly Wiktionary-sourced citation. Put together: \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{noon having passed}\textquotedblright{} — afternoon is, quite literally, the time after noon is done.

\begin{culture}
Here's the honest structural contrast: Telugu's own afternoon word (TE-C28, \textbf{\te{మధ్యాహ్నం}}) is the exact \textbf{same word} as its \textquotedblleft{}noon,\textquotedblright{} simply \textbf{widened} to also cover \textquotedblleft{}afternoon\textquotedblright{} — one word, stretched. Malayalam does something structurally different: \textbf{\ml{ഉച്ച}} itself stays put, meaning only \textquotedblleft{}noon,\textquotedblright{} and a \textbf{second word} — \ml{കഴിഞ്ഞ്}, \textquotedblleft{}passed\textquotedblright{} — gets bolted on to build a new phrase for \textquotedblleft{}afternoon.\textquotedblright{} Same problem (naming the stretch of time after noon), two genuinely different solutions: semantic widening in Telugu, compositional phrase-building in Malayalam.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}uchakaḻiññ\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}afternoon,\textquotedblright{} literally \textquotedblleft{}noon having passed\textquotedblright{}
  \item the verb behind it — kaḻiyuka, \textquotedblleft{}to be over, spent\textquotedblright{} — Proto-Dravidian \emph{kaẓi}
  \item the honest contrast — Telugu widens the same noon-word; Malayalam builds a new phrase on top of it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{ഉച്ചകഴിഞ്ഞ്} literally mean? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Noon having passed\textquotedblright{}} — \ml{ഉച്ച}, \textquotedblleft{}noon,\textquotedblright{} plus the past tense of \textbf{\ml{കഴിയുക}}, \textquotedblleft{}to be over, spent.\textquotedblright{}) Is \ml{ഉച്ചകഴിഞ്ഞ്} a single dictionary word, like \ml{ഉച്ച} itself? (\textbf{No} — it's a transparent two-word phrase; no Wiktionary entry exists for the compound as a whole.) How does Malayalam's strategy for naming \textquotedblleft{}afternoon\textquotedblright{} differ from Telugu's? (\textbf{Telugu widens its existing noon-word's meaning; Malayalam instead builds a new phrase, keeping the noon-word unchanged.})
\end{tcolorbox}
